newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Ex-warlord Taylor installed as Liberian president.
newsitem.headline: Ex-warlord Taylor installed as Liberian president.

text.p: Former warlord Charles Taylor was sworn in on Saturday as Liberia's elected president in a euphoric climax to a transition from seven years of civil war.
A 21-gun salute by African peacekeepers boomed across the capital Monrovia and fighter jets flew past as Taylor took the oath of office from Chief Justice Francis Johnson-Morris.
Thousands of Liberians cheered and danced in the streets of the war-battered capital, spruced up for the ceremony.
About a dozen heads of state or their envoys witnessed the colourful ceremony in Centennial Pavilion commemorating the founding of Liberia by freed American slaves in 1847.
Among them were Nigerian military ruler General Sani Abacha, Ivory Coast President Henri Konan Bedie and the heads of state of Burkina Faso, Chad, Mali, Guinea, Guinea Bissau and Niger.

Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi, widely accused of training and funding Taylor's guerrillas who launched the war, sent his justice minister. South Africa's Nelson Mandela was represented by his Home Affairs Minister Mangosuthu Buthelezi.
High-level envoys represented the United States, the United Nations, Gambia and Taiwan, an important Taylor ally.

"The event here today is the culmination of the collective efforts of the sub-region to restore peace to Liberia," Abacha said in a speech on behalf of regional leaders who brokered peace in Liberia. Abacha heads the 16-nation Economic Community of West African States, which sent troops to Liberia in 1990.
Abacha sounded a warning about the region's new crisis in Sierra Leone, where coup leaders are defying regional efforts to restore the elected government toppled on May 25.
Nigerian troops are enforcing regional economic sanctions against the junta in Freetown. Negotiations to resolve the crisis peacefully collapsed in Ivory Coast this week.
"There cannot be peace and stability in Liberia if Sierra Leone is not stable," Abacha said, calling for international support for the embargo.

In 1989 Taylor launched the civil war that devastated the country that prided itself as Africa's first modern republic. But Liberians looking for strong leadership after the conflict voted massively for him in presidential elections on July 19.

Taylor polled more than 75 percent of votes in the presidential election, crushing 11 rivals. In the parallel legislative poll, his National Patriotic Party swept 21 of the 26 Senate seats and 49 of the 64 in the House of Representives.
In a reassuring gesture, two other former warlords whose militia battled Taylor's guerrillas in Monrovia last year -- George Boley and Roosevelt Johnson -- attended the inauguration.
Taylor in his speech preached reconciliation and respect for human rights, key demands by Liberia's donor countries.
"I pledge here before man and God that there will be no witch-hunting against any citizen and by anyone," he said after taking the oath of office for a six-year term.
He said he was setting up a human rights and reconciliation commission to mediate between former rivals, stressing the need for forgiveness among Liberians.
Among the dignitaries in the pavillion was William Tolbert Jnr, a son of Liberia's last president from the descendants of freed slaves or Americo-Liberians as they are commonly called.
President Tolbert was killed in a 1980 coup led by then master sergeant Samuel Doe, who became the last elected president in 1985.
Doe's alleged rigging of those elections precipitated the chain of events leading to the civil war in which he was captured by guerrillas and tortured to death in September 1990.
Taylor, 49, is an Americo-Liberian.
